Year 8 Enquiry • 1783–1914

The Second British Empire (1783–1914)

Naval Hegemony, De-industrialisation, The 1857 Rebellion & The Scramble for Africa
Visual Decoding • 4 Core Features Walter Crane (1886)

Published for Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, Walter Crane illustrated British global dominion, placing Britannia enthroned atop the world surrounded by colonial subjects:

1. Global Sovereignty:
Britannia enthroned with trident and shield, commanding world oceans with the British lion.
2. Imperial Red Shading:
Every colony tinted red on Mercator projection, exaggerating British worldwide territory.
3. Naval Sea Lanes:
Global steam trade routes guarded by Royal Navy ironclads, asserting industrial hegemony.
4. Subordinated Peoples:
Colonial subjects depicted bearing commodities, legitimising racial hierarchy as natural order.
Red Shading
Dominance on global Mercator maps.
Britannia’s Trident
Naval supremacy under Two-Power Standard.
Labouring Subjects
Moral justification for resource extraction.
Disciplinary Significance: In late 19th-century Britain, popular cartography transformed colonial conquest into a glorious imperial federation, hiding the violent realities of exploitation behind colourful patriotic propaganda.
Key Discussion Question: Evaluation
Does this map celebrate a cooperative global commonwealth of mutual progress, or does it disguise a coercive racial empire sustained by naval dominance and economic extraction?
Primary Visual Evidence: Imperial Federation: Map of the World Showing the Extent of the British Empire in 1886 • Walter Crane BRITISH LIBRARY ARCHIVE • MAPS 957.(46.)
Course Specification • Key Enquiry Sequence Learnt Revised
Enquiry 1: Engines of Empire: Mercantilism, Naval Hegemony & Portsmouth Dockyard (1783–1889)
How was the British Empire built and sustained through maritime industrial power?
Enquiry 2: The De-industrialisation of India: The Company & Handloom Crisis (1700–1850)
How did British corporate rule transform India from the world’s textile workshop into a captive market?
Enquiry 3: The 1857 Indian Rebellion: Sepoy Grievance, Rani Lakshmibai & The Raj (1848–1858)
Was the 1857 Indian Rebellion a limited military mutiny or a war for national liberation?
Enquiry 4: The Scramble for Africa & Imperial Ideology: Maxim Guns & Plunder (1884–1920)
Why did European powers partition Africa after 1884, and was it a civilising mission or armed resource theft?
Enquiry 5: The Imperial Verdict: Workshop of the World or Age of Exploitation? (1851–1901)
Did the British Empire bring global modernisation and order, or economic exploitation and devastation?
Between 1783 and 1914, Britain ruled a quarter of the globe through industrial manufacturing, naval supremacy, and colonial extraction. 1/16
ENQUIRY 1 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

How did naval power and Portsmouth Dockyard sustain the British Empire?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1783–1805 • How did Navigation Acts enrich British ports through colonial trade?
Stage 2 1805–1815 • How did Admiral Nelson’s tactics win sea control at Trafalgar in 1805?
Stage 3 1815–1850 • Why was Portsmouth Royal Dockyard vital to Britain’s naval power?
Stage 4 1860 • How did HMS Warrior make wooden battleships outdated in 1860?
Stage 5 1889 • What did the 1889 Two-Power Standard require from the Royal Navy?
2/16 Portsmouth Royal Dockyard was the industrial beating heart of the British Empire, building the ironclads that commanded the oceans.

Question 2: Explain Why [12 marks • 15 mins]

Extended Writing Practice
Explain why maritime naval supremacy and industrial dockyards were vital for sustaining the British Empire in the 19th century. [12 marks]
Stimulus: The industrial manufacturing capacity of Portsmouth Royal Dockyard The technological breakthrough of HMS Warrior (1860) and the Two-Power Standard (Support each factor with your own precise historical evidence)
Analytical Connectives: One main reason was that... • For example, ... • This was important because... • Another key factor was... • In particular, ... • Overall, the most decisive reason was... because...
Key Vocabulary Bank: Portsmouth Dockyard • HMS Warrior • Two-Power Standard • mercantilism • ironclad • Royal Navy • Pax Britannica • naval supremacy
Task: Using the vocabulary and connectives above, write your analytical response below:
Key Terms / Spellings: 1. 2. 3. 4.
Without Portsmouth’s industrial manufacturing supremacy, Victorian Britain could never have projected global Pax Britannica. 3/16
ENQUIRY 2 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

How did East India Company rule ruin India’s world-leading textile industry?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1650–1700 • How did Mughal India become the world’s leading cloth workshop?
Stage 2 1700–1721 • Why did Parliament pass the 1700 and 1721 Calico Acts against Indian cloth?
Stage 3 August 1765 • How did the 1765 Diwani let the Company buy Indian silk without silver?
Stage 4 1800–1830 • How did Lancashire mills and 70% border taxes ruin Indian weavers?
Stage 5 1834–1850 • How did collapsing cloth exports affect weaving towns like Dhaka by 1834?
4/16 Before British rule, India produced 25% of the world’s manufactured goods; by 1947, colonial de-industrialisation reduced that share to under 2%.

Question 2: Explain Why [12 marks • 15 mins]

Extended Writing Practice
Explain why the Indian textile industry experienced rapid de-industrialisation between 1757 and 1850. [12 marks]
Stimulus: The invention of steam-powered cotton spinning and weaving in Lancashire The unequal tariff regime imposed by the British Parliament (Support each factor with your own precise historical evidence)
Analytical Connectives: One main reason was that... • For example, ... • This was important because... • Another key factor was... • In particular, ... • Overall, the most decisive reason was... because...
Key Vocabulary Bank: De-industrialisation • captive market • Calico Acts • Dhaka muslin • tariff disparity • Lancashire cotton • Diwani • Lord William Bentinck
Task: Using the vocabulary and connectives above, write your analytical response below:
Key Terms / Spellings: 1. 2. 3. 4.
Governor-General Bentinck admitted the truth in 1834: "The bones of the cotton-weavers are bleaching the plains of India." 5/16
ENQUIRY 3 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

Why did corporate military rule spark the 1857 Rebellion and establish the British Raj?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1848–1856 • Why did Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse and seizing Awadh anger Indians?
Stage 2 April–May 1857 • Why did greased Enfield rifle cartridges alarm Hindu and Muslim sepoys?
Stage 3 May–July 1857 • How did the 1857 Meerut mutiny and march on Delhi unite rebels?
Stage 4 1857–1858 • How did Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi lead rebel forces until June 1858?
Stage 5 August 1858 • How did the Government of India Act 1858 change how Britain ruled India?
6/16 Rani Lakshmibai declared "I shall not give up my Jhansi!" and died fighting on horseback, respected even by her British adversaries.

Question 2: Explain Why [12 marks • 15 mins]

Extended Writing Practice
Explain why the 1857 Indian Rebellion broke out and spread rapidly across northern India. [12 marks]
Stimulus: Lord Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse and the annexation of Awadh The introduction of the greased Enfield rifle cartridge in 1857 (Support each factor with your own precise historical evidence)
Analytical Connectives: One main reason was that... • For example, ... • This was important because... • Another key factor was... • In particular, ... • Overall, the most decisive reason was... because...
Key Vocabulary Bank: Sepoy • Doctrine of Lapse • Awadh • Enfield rifle • Rani Lakshmibai • Bahadur Shah Zafar • Azamgarh Proclamation • British Raj • Queen Victoria
Task: Using the vocabulary and connectives above, write your analytical response below:
Key Terms / Spellings: 1. 2. 3. 4.
The 1857 Rebellion proved that corporate rule could not survive; Parliament terminated the East India Company to inaugurate the British Raj. 7/16

ENQUIRY 4 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

How did European industrial powers partition Africa, and how was conquest justified?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1884–1885 • Why did fourteen Western nations meet in Berlin in 1884 with no Africans?
Stage 2 1884 • How did the rule of Effective Occupation speed up inland conquest?
Stage 3 1884–1898 • How did quinine medicine and Maxim guns enable conquest in Africa?
Stage 4 1899 • How did Rudyard Kipling’s 1899 poem try to justify overseas conquest?
Stage 5 1920 • How did King Leopold II’s rubber quotas cause terror across the Congo?
10/16 Hilaire Belloc captured the brutal technological reality of the Scramble: "Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim Gun, and they have not."

Question 2: Explain Why [12 marks • 15 mins]

Extended Writing Practice
Explain why European powers were able to partition and conquer 90% of Africa between 1884 and 1914. [12 marks]
Stimulus: The rules established at the 1884–85 Berlin West Africa Conference Technological breakthroughs including the Maxim machine gun and quinine (Support each factor with your own precise historical evidence)
Analytical Connectives: One main reason was that... • For example, ... • This was important because... • Another key factor was... • In particular, ... • Overall, the most decisive reason was... because...
Key Vocabulary Bank: Scramble for Africa • Berlin Conference • Effective Occupation • Maxim gun • quinine • Battle of Omdurman • Rudyard Kipling • E. D. Morel • resource extraction
Task: Using the vocabulary and connectives above, write your analytical response below:
Key Terms / Spellings: 1. 2. 3. 4.
E. D. Morel exposed the truth: European powers were driven not by a moral civilising mission, but by an insatiable lust for rubber, gold, and palm oil. 11/16
ENQUIRY 5 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

How and why do historians disagree fiercely over the legacy of the British Empire?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1851 • What did the 1851 Great Exhibition and Koh-i-Noor diamond show?
Stage 2 1870–1900 • Why did British engineers build 25,000 miles of railways across India?
Stage 3 1876–1900 • Why did ten million Indians starve while grain was shipped to Britain?
Stage 4 1901 • What did Dadabhai Naoroji’s "Drain of Wealth" argument prove in 1867?
Stage 5 Historiography • How do Niall Ferguson and Shashi Tharoor disagree over the Empire?
12/16 Dadabhai Naoroji, Britain’s first Indian MP, used official British records to prove that colonial taxation bled India of industrial capital.

Question 2: Explain Why [12 marks • 15 mins]

Extended Writing Practice
Explain why the overall impact of the British Empire remains a subject of intense historical debate today. [12 marks]
Stimulus: The construction of modern global infrastructure including railways, telegraphs, and ports Dadabhai Naoroji’s Drain of Wealth theory and recurring late Victorian colonial famines (Support each factor with your own precise historical evidence)
Analytical Connectives: One main reason was that... • For example, ... • This was important because... • Another key factor was... • In particular, ... • Overall, the most decisive reason was... because...
Key Vocabulary Bank: Drain of Wealth • Dadabhai Naoroji • Crystal Palace • Great Exhibition • famine • infrastructure • railways • Optimist vs Pessimist • historiography
Task: Using the vocabulary and connectives above, write your analytical response below:
Key Terms / Spellings: 1. 2. 3. 4.
To Optimists, the Empire brought railways and global trade; to Pessimists, it was an engine of resource extraction and de-industrialisation. 13/16

Historian Writing & Progress Descriptors (Emerging → Greater Depth) 5-BAND PROGRESS SCALE
Emerging (Em)
Identifies key names, dates, and terms; describes what happened using structured frames.
Emerging+ (Em+)
Describes reasons why events occurred; begins to explain causes supported by accurate facts.
Expected (Ex)
Constructs structured paragraphs explaining causes and consequences with precise evidence.
Expected+ (Ex+)
Weighs competing factors and interpretations; explains why key causes were decisive.
Greater Depth (GD)
Crafts sustained, analytical arguments reaching a substantiated historical judgement.
